restrictions: Ordinary collision construction for the complete 64-round SHA-256 hash (sha256-r64-prefix-v1) on 52-byte one-block messages P || BE256(u) with a fixed public 20-byte prefix; 64 is the full SHA-256 round count. No complete collision is exhibited and the attack is not executed at full scale.

time_log2 and memory_log2_bytes are worst-case bounds derived from the fixed program image on a load/store machine with a declared file of 1,024 registers of 256 bits whose 32768 bytes are included in the memory bound; every computed-address access is charged, each evaluation is charged one complete compression through its explicit word operations, and the rare stage-2 work is bounded by a counted budget enforced by a halt. Instruction fetch is not charged as a primitive operation; charging it at one 256-bit load per 32 bytes of kernel code adds 0.1689 bits (the complete ledger recomputed, proof Section L.6), giving 124.48429, which is above both comparators, so this entry's advantage depends on that declared convention. The comparators at this target declare the same convention. The normalized objective is 124.31538 because memory is below 2^20 bytes.

success_probability rests on the random-function theorem of proof Section P (certified lower bound 0.390036155778183, a margin of 0.000036155778 over 0.39, recomputed inside the organizer's executor by the declared experiment sha256-r64-success-bound-v1) and on the declared heuristic H1. The two slice experiments are diagnostic evidence about the fixed target under a public, fixed organizer seed with no holdout and with widths chosen by us; they carry no coverage, confidence or calibration claim. The 16-bit machine experiment is implementation and cost evidence only.

heuristics.statement: For the fixed walk f(u) = S(u) XOR PD, where S(u) is the working state after step 63 of the single compression of M(u) = P || BE256(u) at the complete 64-round SHA-256, the success probability of the frozen algorithm over its uniform offset rho is at least the random-function lower bound of proof Section P (certified value 0.390036155778183), and in particular at least 0.39.
heuristics.scope: Transfers the random-function theorem of proof Section P to the fixed SHA-256 target. The algorithm is generic: it uses no property of SHA-256 beyond evaluating it, and the proof uses only that answers to fresh queries along the lane-serialized search are uniform and independent of the history.
heuristics.extrapolation: Experiments sha256-r64-slice-first-collision-w20-v1 and sha256-r64-slice-first-collision-w24-v1 exercise the first-duplicate mechanism on 512 independent 20- and 24-bit slices of the fixed target, with the same kernel, consecutive starts and lane serialization as the search. The model probability of a returned pair is fixed before execution by exact rational arithmetic at 0.448648 and 0.237789 (114.85 and 60.87 of 256); in our own runs of the organizer's harness the counts were 119 and 54, and the official evaluation runs them again. These are DIAGNOSTIC and not a calibrated confirmation of this premise: the organizer seed material is public and fixed, there is no holdout nonce and no pre-registration, and the widths, slot counts and the choice of these two experiments were ours, so no coverage, confidence statement, false-alarm rate or rejection rule is claimed. The step from the random-function theorem to this fixed target is an exchange of quantifiers, from an average over the random function for every offset to an average over the single offset for one fixed function, which this package assumes and does not prove.
heuristics.limitations: Plausible, not established. The random-function bound exceeds 0.39 by only 0.000036155778, so any fixed-target deficit larger than that defeats the claim. No experiment of this kind at any feasible width can detect a deficit of that size, and a failure would not by itself distinguish a kernel error from non-randomness. The experiments do not reach the full-width distinguished-point and key events or the full function rather than its slices. The random-function argument is the integrated detection-delay bound of our entry 09fe5fcd, itself re-derived from the public proof of 76ab339a; it has been reviewed by its authors and by a fresh-context advisory critic only.

heuristics.statement: The cost model's 256-bit word RAM is realized as a load/store machine with a fixed, declared file of 1,024 registers of 256 bits. Registers are named statically by instruction fields, never reached by a computed address, and the file's 32768 bytes are included in memory_log2_bytes as storage; a register operand is not a load or a store. Every other word (the endpoint table, the lane metadata and the COMP working state) is memory, reached only by charged loads and stores. The algorithm is the fixed program image of proof Section 3.2 (411680 bytes), counted in memory; instruction fetch is not a primitive operation of the cost model and is not charged. COMP is one compression unit plus 64 word operations of block assembly.
heuristics.scope: Accounting convention for proof Sections 3, M and L. The deterministic event bounds and the hash-evaluation counts do not depend on it; the main-loop operation count does.
heuristics.extrapolation: The declared experiment asserts, in the organizer's executor, the kernel's 97218 instructions and 907 registers, the fit of all 957 statically named registers in the declared file, the image round trip and size, and every per-handler closed form measured at the full-width parameters. The contract fixes no register count.
heuristics.limitations: The register-file size is this entry's declaration; the benchmark contract neither fixes nor bounds it, so the time bound is conditional on accepting a 1,024-register file. Instruction fetch is not charged; charging it at one 256-bit load per 32 bytes of kernel code adds 0.1689 bits (complete ledger recomputed, proof Section L.6) and would place this entry above both comparators, so the advantage depends on this convention. Smaller files require spill code in the kernel; no numeric bound for smaller files is claimed for this gate network, because the predecessor's spill curve was measured on a different gate network and was not re-measured here.

heuristics.statement: The generated kernel (97,218 gates, register-allocated as a 97218-instruction listing with 0 output moves and no complement) computes the planes of f(u) from the planes of u for every 256-bit input u.
heuristics.scope: Correctness of the bitsliced main-loop evaluation, on which the success-probability argument depends. Recovery and the final check use the scalar compression and recompute the collision explicitly, so a kernel error cannot produce a false output; it could only cause a missed or spurious endpoint.
heuristics.extrapolation: The declared experiment checks every gate-construction rule exhaustively on all operand classes (12,023 cases over all input assignments, including the Ch multiplexer and the majority carry), proves statically that the register-allocated listing computes the gate DAG for every input, pins the explicit scalar reference to the canonical library SHA-256 on 74 inputs (which fixes the message encoding, padding, endianness and feed-forward), and compares sampled kernel lanes with that reference on all 256 output bits in every trial.
heuristics.limitations: Within this package the composition step (that the builder applies the FIPS 180-4 operations in specification order) is established by inspection and by sampling, not mechanically. Kernel correctness on all 2^256 inputs is not established by any organizer-executed experiment.
